title: Post-Conference Comments of Hamza Yousaf on the Annual Commissioner-Led Reliability Technical Conference under AD26-8.

documents.name: FERC_Comment_AD26-8-000_Hamza_Yousaf.pdf
documents.text:
October 21, 2026

Ms. Debbie-Anne A. Reese
Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, NE
Washington, DC 20426

Re: Docket No. AD26-8-000 — Post-Conference Comments on the Annual Commissioner-Led
Reliability Technical Conference (October 21, 2026)

Dear Secretary Reese:

I respectfully submit these comments in response to the Annual Commissioner-Led Reliability
Technical Conference convened on October 21, 2026, which I attended in person at the Commission’s
headquarters in Washington, DC. I write as a data scientist and doctoral candidate whose research is
directly focused on the reliability challenges discussed at this conference.

I hold a Master of Science in Data Analytics from Mercer University and am currently pursuing a
Doctor of Business Administration at National Louis University, where my dissertation research
evaluates deep learning architectures for AI-driven demand forecasting in U.S. energy utility
operations. I also serve as a Data Scientist at beMatrix USA, where I develop machine learning models
and advanced analytics solutions. My comments draw on both my academic research and
professional experience in applied artificial intelligence.

I. The Urgency of Advanced Load Forecasting for AI-Driven Data Center Loads
The conference underscored that load forecasting has become the single most critical reliability
challenge facing the Bulk-Power System. As NERC President and CEO Jim Robb emphasized during
the conference, accurate load forecasting is essential so that grid operators can anticipate what to
expect in both near-term and longer planning horizons. Multiple panelists confirmed that the
demand patterns from data centers are highly unpredictable: loads can rise and drop suddenly, and
stated capacity plans often diverge substantially from actual utilization.

My doctoral research directly addresses this challenge. Traditional statistical forecasting methods
(e.g., ARIMA, exponential smoothing) were designed for demand patterns that follow seasonal and
cyclical regularities. The volatile, non-linear load profiles introduced by AI compute campuses and
hyperscale data centers fundamentally violate these assumptions. Deep learning architectures,
including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs), and
Transformer-based models, offer the ability to capture complex temporal dependencies, sudden
regime shifts, and non-stationary patterns that characterize these new loads.

I respectfully urge the Commission to consider encouraging investment in and adoption of AI-based
forecasting tools by utilities, RTOs, and ISOs as a component of reliability planning. Specifically:
     • The Commission should consider whether existing reliability standards adequately address the
    need for validated, data-driven forecasting models that can accommodate the rapid emergence
    and volatile nature of AI-driven loads.
    • NERC and regional entities should evaluate the incorporation of machine learning-based
    forecasting benchmarks into model validation requirements, ensuring that planning models
    reflect the operational reality of non-firm, flexible, and curtailable loads.

II. Load Classification and Prioritization of AI Data Center Workloads
A key insight from the conference was the distinction drawn by Dr. Varun Sivaram of Emerald AI
between traditional data center loads and the emerging class of AI compute loads. Dr. Sivaram noted
that AI-driven data center loads are fundamentally different from traditional data center operations:
AI workloads can be categorized by criticality and temporal flexibility. For instance, batch inference
and model training workloads can tolerate interruption or geographic rerouting, whereas mission-
critical real-time inference cannot.

This classification framework has direct implications for grid reliability and resource adequacy
planning. If grid operators and data center operators can jointly categorize AI workloads by their
deferability and curtailability, it becomes possible to design demand response programs tailored to
the computational characteristics of these loads rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

I recommend that the Commission encourage the development of a standardized taxonomy for AI
and data center load classifications. Such a taxonomy would support more granular load modeling,
enable targeted demand response, and improve the accuracy of resource adequacy assessments. AI-
based classification models could automate this categorization in real time, dynamically adjusting
load priority based on grid conditions.

III. Capacity Commitments, Utilization Gaps, and Financial Accountability
Panelists noted a significant gap between committed capacity and actual utilization by data center
operators. It was observed that many data centers operate at approximately 60% capacity while
planning for 90%, creating misalignment between infrastructure investment by utilities and actual
demand. This utilization gap imposes real costs on ratepayers and grid operators who must provision
generation and transmission resources based on stated, rather than realized, demand.

The suggestion that financial commitment mechanisms, such as capacity deposits or take-or-pay
arrangements, could align incentives is well-founded. I further suggest that predictive analytics could
help quantify the probability of load materialization for specific interconnection requests, providing
both utilities and regulators with a data-driven basis for evaluating whether stated capacity needs
are likely to be realized. Such models could draw on historical patterns of data center ramp-up
timelines, utilization trajectories, and technology-specific load factors.

IV. Integration of Renewable and Ancillary Resources as Variable-Load Complements
 The conference highlighted that as loads become more variable, resources must also become more
variable and responsive. Panelists discussed the increasing importance of integrating renewable
energy sources, particularly solar photovoltaic systems, as contributors to grid reliability. The role of
ancillary services, including fast-frequency response and synthetic inertia from battery energy
storage systems, was discussed as essential to managing the grid dynamics introduced by both large
intermittent loads and inverter-based resources.

From a forecasting perspective, the co-optimization of variable generation and variable demand
requires advanced modeling capabilities that can simultaneously forecast both supply-side
renewable output and demand-side AI workload fluctuations. Multi-output deep learning models,
including attention-based architectures, are well-suited to this task and represent a meaningful area
for research and operational deployment.

V. Communication, Coordination, and Risk Acceptance
The discussion on improving communication between utilities, RTOs/ISOs, and large load customers
is critical. Mr. Robb’s call for good models, good data, better planning, model validation, and
improved communication across entities captures the essential requirements. I would add that
standardized data-sharing frameworks between data center operators and grid operators,
potentially facilitated through secure API-based telemetry, would significantly improve both
forecasting accuracy and operational coordination.

The question of acceptable risk levels raised during the conference is fundamentally a question that
can be informed by probabilistic modeling. AI-based risk assessment tools can provide grid operators
with probabilistic forecasts and confidence intervals rather than point estimates, enabling more
informed decision-making about resource commitments and operational reserves.

VI. Conclusion
The challenges discussed at this conference, including volatile and unpredictable data center loads,
the integration of inverter-based resources, declining system inertia, and the need for improved load
forecasting, are precisely the challenges that advanced AI and deep learning methods are designed
to address. I commend the Commission for convening this important discussion and respectfully urge
continued attention to the role that artificial intelligence and machine learning can play in enhancing
the reliability and security of the Bulk-Power System.

I appreciate the opportunity to participate in and comment on these proceedings.

Respectfully submitted,


Hamza Yousaf
PhD data Sciences, Harrisburg University of Science and Technology
M.S. Business Analytics, Mercer University
Data Analyst, beMatrix USA
